title: Selecting and soaking willow
subtitle: How to choose, buy, and prepare willow rods for basket weaving
excerpt: Willow for basket weaving comes in three main types: brown, buff, and white. Each is suited to different uses. This article covers what the terms mean, how to buy the right material, and the soaking times that make willow workable without breaking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Unpeeled, air-dried willow rod. The bark remains on; it is the most robust of the three willow types and is used for stakes and structural work.
Willow that has been boiled and peeled; the bark pigment tans the rods to a warm honey colour. More flexible than brown willow of the same diameter.
Willow that has been peeled fresh, leaving a cream-white surface. The most flexible of the three types; used for fine work and white-on-brown contrast.

content.text: Willow rods for basket weaving are sold dried and must be rehydrated before use. The three types available to buy in Britain are
brown willow
buff willow
, and
white willow
. Each is made differently and has different properties.
Brown willow

Brown willow is the dried, unpeeled rod. The rods are harvested in winter, bundled, and air-dried in a barn or shed. The bark stays on and dries to a mottled brown-grey. Brown willow is the stiffest of the three types because the bark adds structural integrity to the rod. It is used for stakes and for structural baskets that need to hold their shape without flexing. It has the longest soaking time.
Buff willow

Buff willow is boiled for eight to twelve hours in a long tank, then peeled while the bark is loose. The boiling extracts tannins from the bark and drives them into the wood, turning the peeled surface a warm amber-tan. Buff is more flexible than brown at the same diameter and soaks faster. It is the most common material for the siding of domestic baskets. The colour is pleasant and darkens to a rich brown over years of use.
White willow

White willow is peeled fresh in early spring when the sap is rising and the bark slips easily. The peeled surface dries white to cream. White is the most flexible of the three and requires the shortest soaking time. It is the traditional material for fine work: light shopping baskets, flower baskets, and the decorative white-on-brown striped patterns in traditional Somerset willow work. It is the most expensive of the three types.
Buying willow

Willow is sold by the bolt (a bundle of rods tied at both ends and the middle). A bolt is 36 inches in circumference at the base. Rods are sold by length in feet: 3 ft, 4 ft, 5 ft, 6 ft. For a first bread basket, buy a bolt of 4 ft brown and a bolt of 4 ft buff. The 4 ft length suits most stakes and weavers in a 30 cm basket.
Soaking times
Brown willow, 4 ft: soak 8 to 12 hours in cold water. Mellow (wrapped in damp cloth) for 1 to 2 hours after soaking.
Buff willow, 4 ft: soak 4 to 6 hours in cold water. Mellow for 1 hour.
White willow, 4 ft: soak 1 to 2 hours in cold water. Mellow for 30 minutes.
Longer rods need proportionally more soaking time: a 6 ft brown rod may need 16 to 18 hours.
How to tell when the willow is ready

Take a rod and bend it into a U shape. It should bend smoothly without cracking or checking. If the bend cracks, the rod needs more time in the trough or a further hour of mellowing. Over-soaked willow (more than 24 hours) becomes limp and loses its structural spring; the weave will be loose and the finished basket will sag.
